record.statement: Prove that every finite group of prime order is cyclic.

record.query: If G is a finite group of prime order p then G is cyclic.
results_summary: The theorem-search results did not return the target theorem directly but returned Cauchy's theorem variants: if a prime p divides |G|, then G contains an element of order p. This would imply the target when |G|=p, but it is stronger than needed.
Web/background search identified the standard elementary route: choose a nonidentity element, consider its generated cyclic subgroup, use Lagrange's theorem to force its order to be p.
The proof blueprint will not cite Cauchy's theorem or any external paper as a black box; it will prove the needed Lagrange lemma directly by cosets.

useful_references.title: Lagrange's theorem (group theory) background
useful_references.complete_statement: If H is a subgroup of a finite group G, then |H| divides |G|; equivalently, |G|=[G:H]|H| where [G:H] is the number of left cosets of H in G.
expanded_definitions: A left coset of H in G has the form gH={gh:h in H}.
The index [G:H] is the number of distinct left cosets of H in G.
applicability_check: The target group is finite, and the subgroup generated by any element is a subgroup, so Lagrange's theorem applies once proved.
partial_result_analysis: No extra hypotheses beyond finiteness and the subgroup condition are needed for the Lagrange lemma. The target adds the prime-order hypothesis to force the divisor to be p rather than another proper divisor.
proof_insights: Prove Lagrange by showing left cosets partition G and each coset has the same cardinality as H.
useful_references.why_useful: It identifies the standard elementary sublemma needed for a self-contained proof.

record.query: If H is a subgroup of a finite group G then the order of H divides the order of G.
results_summary: The theorem search returned several statements of Lagrange's theorem, including arXiv:0907.5587 Theorem A.1.11 and arXiv:0811.3959 Theorem 3.1.
These results confirm that the intended key claim is Lagrange's theorem, but the blueprint will include a direct proof by cosets rather than relying on an external paper theorem.

useful_references.title: Systematic analysis of finite family symmetry groups and their application to the lepton sector
useful_references.complete_statement: (Lagrange) Let G be a finite group of order n, and H subset G a subgroup of G with order m. Then m is a divisor of n.
useful_references.paper_id: search_arxiv_theorems result title: Systematic analysis of finite family symmetry groups and their application to the lepton sector
expanded_definitions: Here G is a finite group and H is a subgroup; order means cardinality of the finite group or subgroup.
applicability_check: The target proof needs exactly this conclusion for H=<a>. The proof will derive it internally, so no external applicability risk remains.
partial_result_analysis: This is not merely partial for the key subgoal; it is exactly the subgoal. For the main theorem it still needs the additional prime-divisor step.
proof_insights: The standard proof partitions G into equally sized cosets of H.
useful_references.why_useful: It grounds the key lemma selected for the blueprint.

record.summary: Two proof routes were proposed: a self-contained Lagrange/coset route and a shorter Cauchy-theorem route. Direct screening will select the route with the smallest reliable proof obligation.

notes: The proof includes a self-contained Lagrange lemma before the final theorem.
